answer: A WARNING is raised when projected 15-minute demand reaches **1,125 kW** (or when the probability of exceeding the contract in the next hour is at least 20%). This is 90% of the 1,250 kW contract capacity, providing headroom before an over-contract ALARM; normal summer peaks of 1,100–1,180 kW also make this an intentionally close operating threshold. [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-02_demand_management.md#EM-02 Demand Management > Demand status tiers] [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-02_demand_management.md#EM-02 Demand Management > Key terms]

Demand above the 1,250 kW contract capacity is billed on the excess demand: at 2× the period’s contract price up to 10% above the contract, and 3× the contract price for excess beyond that. [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-04_glossary.md#EM-04 Glossary > Billing and demand terms > Exceedance] [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-04_glossary.md#EM-04 Glossary > Billing and demand terms > Contract capacity]

answer: The night-load baseline uses a CUSUM allowance of **k = 0.5 robust sigmas** and an alarm threshold of **h = 8 robust sigmas**. It also requires night load to be more than **3 kW** above expectation before the rule fires. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-04_compressed_air_leak.md#SOP-04 Compressed Air Leak > Trigger]

The forecaster predicts the change from an anchor because its tree models cannot extrapolate beyond values seen in training. Since contract exceedances were rare in training, the earlier absolute-level model tended to miss them. Modelling the increment lets it add heat- or start-up-driven load to the current baseline, improving exceedance warning. For 15 minutes–3 hours the anchor is the last completed interval; for day-ahead it is the same time last week. [source: docs/forecasting.md#Load forecasting > Model]

In summer (16 May–15 October), weekday peak hours are **16:00–22:00**. [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-03_tariff_guide.md#EM-03 Tariff Guide > Time-of-use periods and energy prices > Summer (16 May - 15 October)]

Act before the peak: pre-cool in early afternoon with CH-01 leading and stage CH-02 early; do not manually start a chiller during the peak. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-06_heat_wave_precooling.md#SOP-06 Heat Wave Pre-cooling > Procedure > Step 2: pre-cool]

Hold non-essential start-ups, optional burn-in loading and test runs; use the staggered start order for anything essential. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-06_heat_wave_precooling.md#SOP-06 Heat Wave Pre-cooling > Procedure > Step 3: hold non-essential start-ups]

A ≥20% next-hour exceedance probability is WARNING; ≥50% is ALARM. [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-02_demand_management.md#EM-02 Demand Management > Forecast-based warnings] At WARNING/ALARM, monitor each interval and shed sequentially until projected demand is below the 1,250 kW contract: pause EV charging, delay burn-in loading, raise chilled-water setpoint by 1°C, then lower compressed-air pressure by 0.5 bar. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-03_demand_exceedance_response.md#SOP-03 Demand Exceedance Response > Step 2: shed in playbook order]

Never shed the server room, a molder mid-cycle, or a reflow oven containing boards. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-03_demand_exceedance_response.md#SOP-03 Demand Exceedance Response > Step 2: shed in playbook order] Restore actions one at a time in reverse order only after demand is stable below 1,125 kW.
